assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars. That is what money buys now.

Stocks grow 5.0% a year above inflation on average, and bonds 1.8%. Some years are good and some are bad. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They stay fixed, so every plan faces the same markets. To see a bad stretch, try 'markets fall 30%'.
A market test is one made-up run of the markets, year by year. We test many of them. 'Safe in 90 of 100 market tests' means your money lasts in 90 of every 100.

Until you retire you save about $4,822 a year. That is what your take-home pay leaves after spending. It is less than the 10% of pay assumed. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' or your spending now.
Pay stays the same until you retire. The plan counts no raises, since they are not certain. If your pay changes, update it in your answers.

Social Security is a rough guess from today's pay. We count work from about 22 until you retire. Missing years under 35 count as zero. Your own figure is at ssa.gov/myaccount. Your answers show $25,600 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70. That pays about $31,800 a year.
If you retire before 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until Medicare starts. This is a guess. Other health costs follow US government figures by age.

Tax uses 2027 federal rates, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving lowers your taxable pay. In retirement we count 85% of Social Security as taxed. That is the most the law allows, so tax may run a little high.
The plan runs to age 94. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long. This comes from a US life table. People with more money often live longer.
